title: Teaching and Learning is King, but Curriculum is Queen, and She Wears the Trousers
author: Dominic Salles
summary: Prompted by a podcast on a book of teaching techniques, Dominic Salles asks whether improving teaching misses the point and argues that curriculum matters more. He opens with his school Kingsdown's strong Progress 8 results for students with high attendance and for disadvantaged students, then insists the teachers are good but no better than most. The theatre analogy: great performance depends less on acting than on the script. He lists fifteen curriculum features he credits, including retrieval at the start of every lesson, booklets, knowledge organisers, online quizzing platforms, retrieval homework and a handful of Lemov techniques. His thesis is that you do not need brilliant teachers to get brilliant results, because well-built curriculum carries much of the load. The evidence is one school's results and his own attribution, so the claim is suggestive rather than proven.
points: Salles claims that curriculum design, not teaching technique, is the main lever for results, citing his school's Progress 8 figures.
Great teachers are common, so systems that depend on exceptional teaching are fragile compared with a strong script.
His fifteen features combine retrieval at the start of every lesson, shared booklets and knowledge organisers, and platforms that give instant feedback.
Even the few teaching techniques the school uses are described as curriculum improvements rather than teaching improvements.
League tables of effort and progress are used to counter the relative deprivation effect, so more students see they are doing well.
quotes: But most teachers in most schools are incredible. We work extra hours for no extra pay, we believe in every student’s potential, we go the extra mile. We perform at least 4 hours on stage every day, to a critical, matinee audience who got tickets on the cheap and probably prefer the show next door.
The path to being a great performer, in this analogy, isn’t acting. It’s the script. The curriculum.

But for students who had 95%, Progress 8 was +0.78. For disadvantaged students (excluding EAL students), Progress 8 was +0.65. When we include those with up to 10% absence, missing one day a fortnight, those figures are still +0.53 and +0.19 respectively.
Most departments use booklets, so everything a student needs to know is in one place – and students can teach themselves should they be absent.
If we think of the curriculum as what students study, then the first 4 of these techniques are ways of improving the curriculum, rather than teaching.
You don’t have to be a brilliant teacher to get brilliant results. It’s the curriculum.
